title: Every morning at 7: one-sided headaches behind the left eye in a 30-year-old man in general practice
desc: In this station the candidate takes a focused history from Abdul, a 30-year-old man in general practice, and does a focused neurological and head examination. He is in the middle of an attack of severe pain behind his left eye. The attacks have come almost every day for 2 months, wake him at about 7 am and last 2 to 3 hours. During them his left eye waters and his left nostril runs, and he cannot sit still. In Part 2 the candidate reads his observations, ECG and MRI brain, diagnoses cluster headache, and plans treatment for the attacks, prevention, neurology referral and safety netting, including his mood.
focus: Telling cluster headache apart from other primary and secondary headaches by its pattern and autonomic features, screening for red flags, and starting acute and preventive treatment in general practice
diagnosis: Cluster headache (left-sided, episodic, in a current bout)
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Abdul, a 30-year-old man, has come in with headaches. In the waiting room he is sitting very uncomfortably, holding the left side of his head and rocking back and forth. Your GP supervisor will see him after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Abdul and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Abdul's observations, his ECG and his MRI brain report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Abdul, a 30-year-old man with an office job at the Australian Taxation Office. You are in the middle of an attack. It started at 7 am and it is now about 9 am. You cannot sit still: rock in your chair and hold the left side of your head, and if the candidate lets you, stand up and pace. Keep your answers short because of the pain. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “It's my head again, the left side. I can't stand it anymore.”

The headache (give only when asked):

  • Where: the left side of your head only, deep behind your left eye. It is always on the left.
  • What it feels like: sharp and throbbing.
  • Severity: 10 out of 10, “unbearable”.
  • Today: it started at 7 am and woke you up. It builds up over a few minutes. It did not hit you all at once like a thunderclap.
  • Pattern: almost every day for 2 months, starting at around 7 am and waking you from sleep. It stays constant for 2 to 3 hours, then goes completely, and you have no pain for the rest of the day. If asked whether they are getting worse or more frequent: no, they have been the same since they started 2 months ago.
  • Earlier episodes: about a year ago you had a similar run of these headaches for about 6 weeks. They went away and you were completely fine for about 8 months, until 2 months ago.
  • What makes it worse: “Sitting still seems to make it more obvious, that's why I usually pace around my house, or rock in my chair.”
  • What helps: nothing. You tried Panadol and it does nothing.
  • Triggers: nothing has changed in your lifestyle.

During the attacks (give each only when the candidate asks about it): your left eye waters and goes red, and your left nostril runs and feels blocked. You have not noticed anything else about your face.

Say no if asked about: nausea or vomiting; flashing lights, zigzags or other warning signs before the pain; being bothered by light or noise; a sudden headache that hit like a thunderclap; fever, a stiff neck or a rash; a head injury; blurred, double or lost vision; weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or confusion; a headache that is worse lying down or when you cough, sneeze or strain; weight loss or cancer; jaw pain when chewing or a tender scalp; seizures.

Impact and mood: “I have no idea what this is and it's driving me insane, I really need these headaches to stop, they're really affecting my life.” If asked about your mood: you are worn down and you dread the mornings, but you have no thoughts of harming yourself.

Past medical history: tonsillectomy at 13. Otherwise well.

Medicines: Panadol (tried for the headaches), cough syrup in flu season, and vitamin C. If asked about recreational drugs: marijuana about once every 3 years.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your mother had a gastric bypass for obesity at 54. Your father had similar headaches. You can't remember what they were called, but he took medicine for them. He also has COPD.

Social history:

  • You have smoked a pack a day since you were 20.
  • You drink 3 or 4 drinks a fortnight.
  • You work in an office at the Australian Taxation Office. You go for walks in the afternoon and your diet is mostly healthy.
  • You live in a townhouse with your male partner and your dog. Your partner, your family and your colleagues are supportive.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: you have no idea what it is.
  • Concern: a brain tumour or some other brain disease.
  • Expectation: you need these headaches to stop.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Do I have a brain disease or brain tumour or something? What else could cause this much pain every single day?” Accept an honest, brief answer, or a promise to come back to it once the tests are done.

How you change: towards the end of Part 1 the pain starts to ease, and you can sit a little more still.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: restless, rocking in the chair, holding the left side of his head. Alert and fully oriented. No rash.
  • Observations: the practice nurse has taken them. He is afebrile, his heart rate is at the upper end of normal, and his BP is normal. The full set is handed over in Part 2.
  • Eyes and face, inspected during the attack: left conjunctiva red, with tears running from the left eye. Clear discharge from the left nostril. Mild drooping of the left upper eyelid. The right eye and nostril are normal.
  • Pupils: left 2 mm, right 4 mm. Both react to light directly and consensually. No relative afferent pupillary defect.
  • Fundoscopy: optic discs pink with sharp margins on both sides. No papilloedema. Venous pulsations present.
  • Cranial nerves: visual acuity 6/6 in each eye. Visual fields full to confrontation. Eye movements full with no double vision or nystagmus. Facial sensation normal in V1, V2 and V3 on both sides. Corneal reflex present, if mentioned. Facial movements symmetrical. The other cranial nerves are normal.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power, reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor. Coordination normal.
  • Gait: normal, including heel-to-toe walking.
  • Meningism: no neck stiffness. Kernig's sign negative. No rash.
  • Head and neck: temporal arteries pulsatile and not tender. No scalp tenderness. No tenderness over the sinuses. Full neck movement. Temporomandibular joints normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Abdul's identity, and explains the examination and gains consent.
Acknowledges his severe pain and distress, lets him move or pace rather than insisting he sit still, keeps questions short and focused, and stays non-judgemental about smoking and cannabis.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site: strictly one-sided, on the left, deep behind the left eye.
Character and severity: sharp and throbbing, 10/10.

Timing: today's attack began at 7 am; almost daily for 2 months at about 7 am, waking him from sleep; constant for 2 to 3 hours, then completely gone; a similar 6-week run of attacks about a year ago, followed by about 8 pain-free months.
kids.d: Award only if the time of day, the duration and the pain-free intervals are all established.

kids.x: Aggravating and relieving factors: sitting still makes it worse, so he paces or rocks; Panadol does not help; no lifestyle change.

check.x: Asks about autonomic features on the same side during attacks: a watering or red left eye and a runny or blocked left nostril [present].
check.d: Award only if the candidate asks about both the eye and the nose.

check.x: Asks about migraine features: nausea or vomiting, aura, sensitivity to light or noise [none].
Screens for the red flags of a secondary headache:

kids.x: Asks about sudden thunderclap onset, fever, neck stiffness and rash [none].
kids.d: Award for asking about thunderclap onset plus at least two of fever, neck stiffness and rash.

kids.x: Asks about features of raised intracranial pressure: worse lying down or with coughing or straining, vomiting, visual blurring, steady progression [none]. Explores the waking from sleep and establishes that the attacks come at a fixed time, not as a progressive morning headache.
Asks about focal neurological symptoms, weight loss or cancer, head injury, and jaw claudication or scalp tenderness [none].

check.x: Takes the past medical, medication, drug and allergy history: tonsillectomy at 13; Panadol with no effect, cough syrup in flu season, vitamin C; marijuana about once every 3 years; no allergies.
Takes the family history: father had similar headaches treated with medication, and COPD; mother had a gastric bypass at 54.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking, quantified (a pack a day since 20, about 10 pack-years), and alcohol (3 or 4 drinks a fortnight).
Work, home and supports: office job at the ATO, lives with his male partner and dog in a townhouse, afternoon walks, mostly healthy diet, supportive partner, family and colleagues.
Impact on his life and mood, including thoughts of self-harm [worn down and dreads the mornings; no thoughts of self-harm].

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea what it is, fears a brain tumour or brain disease, needs the headaches to stop.
Examination
Comments on general inspection and asks for the observations, including temperature and BP [restless, rocking, holding the left side of his head; afebrile, HR upper-normal, BP normal].
Inspects the eyes and face during the attack:

kids.x: Left conjunctival redness, tearing from the left eye and a runny left nostril.
Pupils and eyelids: a smaller left pupil with mild left ptosis, both pupils reacting to light, recognised as a partial left Horner's syndrome during the attack.

check.x: Performs fundoscopy, looking for papilloedema [discs normal, no papilloedema].
Examines the cranial nerves: acuity, visual fields, eye movements, facial sensation including V1, and the corneal reflex if mentioned [normal].
Screens the limbs and gait: pronator drift, power, reflexes, plantars, coordination and gait [normal].
Checks for meningism and rash: neck stiffness and Kernig's sign [none].
Palpates the temporal arteries, scalp and sinuses and checks neck movement [normal].
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: during the attack HR 94 and BP 138/86 with pain 10/10, afebrile, SpO2 normal; everything returned to normal as the pain resolved on its own without treatment. No fever, which argues against meningitis.
Interprets the ECG as normal sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval (160 ms) and no conduction block, and states it is the baseline needed before starting verapamil.
Interprets the MRI brain as normal: no mass, haemorrhage or hydrocephalus, normal pituitary and cavernous sinuses, so no structural cause, which answers his fear of a tumour.

Gives cluster headache as the most likely diagnosis, justified by strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 2 to 3 hours, daily at the same time for weeks, waking him from sleep, with same-sided autonomic features and restlessness, in a male smoker with a possible family history, and a normal neurological examination and MRI.

Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case, e.g. migraine, tension-type headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, subarachnoid haemorrhage, a space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure, meningitis or encephalitis, carotid artery dissection, and giant cell arteritis.
check.d: Award for four or more differentials, including at least one primary and two secondary headaches, each with a feature for or against.

check.x: Management
Explains in plain language that this is cluster headache: a recognised primary headache, not a brain tumour (the MRI is normal), that comes in bouts and can be treated.
Plans treatment for the attacks:

kids.x: 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes at the start of an attack, with no smoking near the oxygen.
kids.d: Award only if the high flow and the non-rebreather mask are both stated.

kids.x: Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg at the start of an attack (an intranasal triptan as an alternative), and explains that paracetamol and other oral painkillers do not work for these attacks.

check.x: Plans prevention for the current bout:

kids.x: Verapamil, starting at 80 mg three times daily (or modified-release 240 mg daily) and increased by 80 mg every 1 to 2 weeks as tolerated, with an ECG before each dose increase to check for heart block.
kids.d: Accept verapamil with ECG monitoring without the exact dose.

kids.x: A short course of corticosteroid (prednisolone) as a bridge while the verapamil takes effect.
kids.d: Accept 'a short course' without the exact dose.

check.x: Refers him to a neurologist.
Gives lifestyle advice: stop smoking (brief advice, Quitline 13 7848, offer of pharmacotherapy), avoid alcohol during a bout, and keep a headache diary.
Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words, with 000 or ED: a sudden severe headache unlike his usual attacks, fever with a stiff neck or rash, new weakness, numbness, vision loss, trouble speaking or confusion, or a headache that changes pattern or does not settle; chest pain after sumatriptan that does not settle.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags, with 000 or ED.

check.x: Safety-nets his mood: if he feels hopeless or has thoughts of harming himself, he should see the GP promptly, call Lifeline (13 11 14), or call 000 in an emergency.
Arranges follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks (ECG before each verapamil increase), the neurology appointment, the headache diary and written information.

part2.lead: Your GP supervisor saw Abdul after you, arranged an ECG that morning and an MRI brain, which he had 5 days later, and booked him back to plan treatment. Abdul asked to wait for the scan result before starting any new medicine. A week after his first visit he has returned, still having an attack most mornings. Here are the practice nurse's observations from the first visit, his ECG and his MRI brain report.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: “So it's definitely not a tumour? What is it then, and will it ever stop?”
  • When treatment comes up, ask: “Is there anything that will actually stop an attack? Panadol does nothing.” If oxygen is offered, ask: “I smoke. Is that a problem?”
  • At the fourth question, after the examiner has put it, ask: “What do I do if one comes on tomorrow morning?”

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, first visit)
handover.result: Taken in the treatment room during the attack and repeated as it settled. No treatment was given.
handover.model:
• Read: at 09:05, during the attack, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, HR 94 and regular, BP 138/86, temperature 36.8 °C, alert, pain 10/10. By 09:50 the pain had gone on its own: HR 72, BP 122/78, pain 0. All values are within the normal (white) zone of the NSW adult observation chart, so no escalation is needed.
  • For Abdul: the higher HR and BP during the attack, compared with his settled 72 and 122/78, fit severe pain. He is afebrile, which argues against meningitis or encephalitis. The attack lasted about 3 hours from 7 am and resolved completely without treatment, which fits a self-limiting primary headache attack.
  • What it changes: he is stable and can be managed in general practice.

rows.note: Holding left side of head, pacing; left eye watering
Pain gone on its own; no treatment given; left eye no longer watering, pupils now equal, no ptosis.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (first visit, 10:05)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, recorded at 10:05 on the day of the first visit, after the attack had settled.

  • Rate: 72/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm.
  • Axis: +60 degrees.
  • PR: 160 ms.
  • QRS: 88 ms, normal morphology.
  • QTc: 405 ms.
  • ST and T: no ST elevation or depression; T waves normal.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.
handover.model:
• Read: normal sinus rhythm at 72/min, normal axis, PR 160 ms with no atrioventricular block, normal QRS and QTc, no ischaemic changes. A normal ECG.
  • For Abdul: his conduction is normal, so there is no barrier to verapamil, which can cause bradycardia and heart block. There is no ischaemia, and a 30-year-old with no cardiac history can use a triptan.
  • What it changes: this is the baseline for verapamil. An ECG is repeated before each dose increase to check the PR interval.

handover.label: MRI brain (5 days after the first visit)
handover.result:
Examination: MRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, SWI) before and after intravenous gadolinium, with thin sections through the pituitary fossa and cavernous sinuses.

Clinical details: 30-year-old man with 2 months of near-daily attacks of severe left orbital pain lasting 2 to 3 hours and waking him from sleep, with left lacrimation and rhinorrhoea. A similar bout about a year ago. Normal neurological examination. Exclude a structural cause.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Brain parenchyma: normal grey and white matter signal. No mass, oedema or abnormal enhancement. No restricted diffusion.
  • Haemorrhage: none on SWI.
  • Ventricles and CSF spaces: normal size and configuration. No hydrocephalus. No midline shift.
  • Posterior fossa and craniocervical junction: normal. Cerebellar tonsils in a normal position.
  • Pituitary and cavernous sinuses: pituitary gland normal in size, signal and enhancement. Cavernous sinuses symmetrical and normal.
  • Vessels: normal flow voids in the major intracranial arteries and dural venous sinuses.
  • Orbits and paranasal sinuses: normal orbits. Paranasal sinuses clear.

Conclusion: normal MRI brain with contrast. No intracranial or sellar lesion to account for the headaches.
handover.model:
• Read: normal brain, ventricles, posterior fossa, pituitary, cavernous sinuses and orbits. No mass, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus or abnormal enhancement.
  • For Abdul: there is no structural mimic, such as a pituitary or cavernous sinus lesion, that can produce cluster-like attacks. There is no tumour or raised pressure to explain the headaches that wake him. This answers his fear of a brain tumour.
  • What it changes: it supports a primary headache, so cluster headache can be diagnosed with confidence and treated. No further imaging is needed unless the pattern changes or new signs appear.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Abdul, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Abdul now, here in general practice.
Before Abdul goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; Abdul, 30.
  • Situation: 2 months of near-daily, strictly left orbital attacks (10/10, 2 to 3 hours, waking him at 7 am) with left tearing and runny nose and restlessness; still daily.
  • Background: similar 6-week bout a year ago, then 8 months pain-free; otherwise well; Panadol ineffective; pack a day since 20; father had similar headaches.
  • Assessment: red eye, tearing, rhinorrhoea, mild ptosis and miosis on the left during the attack; no papilloedema, meningism or focal signs. HR 94 and BP 138/86 during the attack (up from his settled 72 and 122/78), consistent with pain; afebrile; settled untreated. ECG normal, PR 160. MRI with contrast normal. Cluster headache.
  • Recommendation: oxygen and SC sumatriptan for attacks; verapamil with ECG monitoring and a steroid bridge; neurology referral; review in 1 to 2 weeks.

Most likely: cluster headache, episodic, in a current bout. For: strictly unilateral orbital pain of 2 to 3 hours, daily at the same time, waking him; same-sided tearing, redness, rhinorrhoea and partial Horner's; restlessness; male smoker; father affected; normal examination and MRI.

  • Migraine: against: no nausea, aura or photophobia; he paces.
  • Tension-type: against: severe, one-sided, autonomic features.
  • Paroxysmal hemicrania: against: one 2 to 3 hour attack a day, not many short ones.
  • SAH: against: recurrent, builds over minutes, no meningism.
  • Tumour or raised ICP: for: wakes him. Against: fixed-time attacks, full resolution, no papilloedema, normal MRI.
  • Meningitis: against: afebrile, no neck stiffness or rash.
  • Carotid dissection: for: unilateral pain with ipsilateral Horner's in a young adult. Against: stereotyped recurrent attacks, Horner's resolves between attacks, no neck pain or trauma.
  • GCA: against: age 30, normal temporal arteries.

1. Explain: cluster headache, not a tumour; it comes in bouts and is treatable.
  2. Attacks: 100% oxygen 12 to 15 L/min via a non-rebreather for 15 minutes at onset; or sumatriptan 6 mg SC, repeat after at least 1 hour if needed, maximum 12 mg in 24 hours. Oral analgesics do not work.
  3. Home oxygen: cylinder with a regulator giving at least 12 L/min and a non-rebreather mask, usually supplied privately; check state program eligibility; smoking is a fire risk and often excludes funding.
  4. Prevention: verapamil 80 mg orally three times daily (or modified-release 240 mg daily), increased by 80 mg every 1 to 2 weeks as tolerated, ECG before each increase; higher doses only under a neurologist. Bridge with prednisolone 50 to 60 mg orally daily for 5 days, then tapered over about 2 weeks.
  5. Refer: neurology.
  6. Lifestyle and mood: quit smoking (Quitline 13 7848, pharmacotherapy); no alcohol during a bout; headache diary; acknowledge the toll and offer support.

• For an attack: start the oxygen or the sumatriptan straight away, at the first sign of pain.
  • Call 000 or go to ED: a sudden severe headache unlike his attacks; fever with a stiff neck or rash; new weakness, numbness, vision loss, trouble speaking or confusion; a headache that changes pattern or does not settle; chest pain after sumatriptan that does not go away.
  • Mood: if he feels hopeless or thinks of harming himself, see the GP promptly, call Lifeline (13 11 14), or call 000 in an emergency.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks with an ECG before each verapamil increase; neurology appointment; headache diary; written information.

ddx.dx: Cluster headache (left-sided, episodic, in a current bout)
ddx.for: Strictly left orbital pain at 10/10, lasting 2 to 3 hours, at the same time almost daily for 2 months and waking him, with same-sided tearing, red eye, rhinorrhoea and partial Horner's, restlessness, an earlier bout a year ago with 8 pain-free months, a father with similar headaches, and a normal examination and MRI.

ddx.against: No nausea, vomiting, aura or sensitivity to light or noise; he paces rather than lying still; attacks are daily and last 2 to 3 hours with marked same-sided autonomic features.

ddx.for: Unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features.
ddx.against: Attacks last 2 to 3 hours (PH 2 to 30 min) and occur once a day rather than many times.
Daily recurrent attacks that build over minutes and resolve completely, with no thunderclap onset, meningism or neurological deficit, and a normal MRI with no blood on SWI.

ddx.dx: Space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure
ddx.for: The headaches wake him from sleep.
ddx.against: Fixed-time attacks with complete resolution, no vomiting, positional or Valsalva features or progression, no papilloedema or focal signs, and a normal MRI with contrast.

ddx.for: Unilateral head pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner's in a young adult.
ddx.against: Recurrent stereotyped attacks over months with full resolution; Horner's resolves between attacks; no neck pain, trauma or focal deficit.

guide:
Part 1:

  • Abdul is in an attack. Play the restlessness: he rocks, holds his head and paces if allowed.
  • Give each autonomic symptom only when the candidate asks about it.
  • Give the examination findings for the eyes and face only when the candidate inspects them. The partial Horner's is present because he is mid-attack. The ptosis and miosis resolved as the attack settled.
  • The observations are summarised in Part 1. The full set is handed over in Part 2.
  • Credit item 8.2 when the candidate explores the waking from sleep and finds that the attacks come at a fixed time and resolve completely. This tells cluster attacks apart from a progressive raised-pressure headache.

Part 2:

  • Hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order.
  • Score item 26 from the differentials question: four or more differentials, including at least one primary and two secondary headaches, each with a feature for or against.
  • Score item 28 when the candidate answers Abdul's “is it a tumour?” question.
  • Score items 29 to 32 from the management answer, and items 34 to 36 from the fourth question.
  • If the candidate raised mood or self-harm in management rather than in the fourth question, credit item 35.

High-performing candidate:

  • Pins down the strict laterality, the clockwork timing, the 2 to 3 hour duration and the pain-free intervals.
  • Asks directly about same-sided eye and nose symptoms and notices the restlessness.
  • Screens the red flags systematically.
  • Inspects the eyes during the attack, examines the fundi and finds no focal signs.
  • In Part 2, uses the normal MRI to reassure Abdul honestly and links the ECG to verapamil.
  • Plans high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreather and SC sumatriptan, starts verapamil with ECG monitoring and a steroid bridge, and refers to neurology.
  • Addresses smoking near oxygen, alcohol and his mood.

Borderline candidate:

  • Labels it migraine without asking about autonomic features.
  • Misses the red-flag screen or omits fundoscopy.
  • Offers oral analgesics or low-flow oxygen.
  • Starts verapamil without mentioning ECG monitoring.
  • Gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Approach to headache: primary or secondary?

Most headaches are primary: migraine, tension-type and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, of which cluster headache is the commonest. The history's first job is to screen for a secondary cause. SNNOOP10 is a useful red-flag list:

  • S: systemic symptoms, including fever.
  • N: a history of neoplasm.
  • N: a neurological deficit.
  • O: sudden or thunderclap onset.
  • O: older age at onset (over 50).
  • P10: a change in pattern or a new headache; positional; precipitated by Valsalva or exercise; papilloedema; progressive or atypical; pregnancy or the postpartum period; a painful eye with autonomic features; post-traumatic; immunosuppression; painkiller overuse.

Abdul's headaches wake him from sleep. This must be explored, not ignored. Here the waking comes from attacks at a fixed time that resolve completely. That is the circadian pattern of cluster headache, not the progressive early-morning headache with vomiting of raised intracranial pressure. A painful eye with autonomic features is itself on the red-flag list, which is one reason to image a first presentation of cluster-like headache.

Why Abdul has cluster headache

The ICHD-3 criteria are at least 5 attacks with all of the following:

  • severe or very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes untreated;
  • one or both of:
    • at least one same-sided autonomic feature: conjunctival injection or lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, forehead or facial sweating, miosis or ptosis;
    • a sense of restlessness or agitation;
  • attacks from one every other day to 8 a day;
  • no better explanation.

Abdul has:

  • strictly left orbital pain at 10/10, lasting 2 to 3 hours;
  • attacks almost daily for 2 months, at about 7 am, waking him;
  • left tearing, redness and rhinorrhoea, and a partial left Horner's during the attack;
  • restlessness: he paces and rocks;
  • an earlier 6-week bout about a year ago, followed by about 8 pain-free months.

He is typical in other ways too: male, a smoker, in his 20s to 40s, and with a father who probably had the same condition. Bouts separated by pain-free remissions of 3 months or more make it episodic cluster headache, as in Abdul. Attacks without such remissions for a year or more make it chronic. The diagnosis is clinical. Bloods do not help.

Differentials

  • Migraine: usually lasts 4 to 72 hours, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia. The patient lies still in a dark room rather than pacing.
  • Tension-type headache: bilateral, pressing and mild to moderate, without autonomic features.
  • Other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: paroxysmal hemicrania has shorter, more frequent attacks and responds completely to indometacin. SUNCT/SUNA attacks last seconds to minutes. These are for the neurologist.
  • Secondary causes to exclude:
    • subarachnoid haemorrhage (thunderclap onset);
    • meningitis or encephalitis (fever, meningism);
    • a space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure (progressive, positional, papilloedema). Pituitary and cavernous sinus lesions can mimic cluster headache;
    • carotid artery dissection (painful Horner's that persists between attacks, or neck pain): needs CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels;
    • giant cell arteritis, which is almost unknown under 50.

The results

  • Observations: show the physiological response to severe pain, with no fever. Everything resolved without treatment.
  • ECG: normal, with a PR of 160 ms. This is the baseline before verapamil, which can cause bradycardia and heart block.
  • MRI brain with contrast: normal, including the pituitary and cavernous sinuses. This excludes a structural mimic and lets you reassure Abdul honestly that he does not have a tumour. A first presentation of cluster-like headache, or any atypical feature, warrants an MRI.

Management (eTG)

  • Acute attacks: oral analgesics act too slowly and do not help.
    • 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes at the start of an attack. Nobody may smoke near oxygen, which is a fire risk.
    • Home oxygen (a cylinder with a regulator giving at least 12 L/min and a non-rebreather mask) is usually supplied privately; check state program eligibility, and note that smoking is a fire risk and often excludes funding, which is another reason to quit.
    • Or sumatriptan 6 mg SC, repeat after at least 1 hour if needed; maximum 12 mg in 24 hours. An intranasal triptan is an alternative, and intranasal lidocaine is an adjunct. Triptans are avoided in coronary or cerebrovascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Prevention during a bout:
    • Verapamil is first line: start verapamil 80 mg orally three times daily (or modified-release 240 mg daily) and increase by 80 mg every 1 to 2 weeks as tolerated, with an ECG before each increase (per eTG). The usual range is 240 to 480 mg daily; higher doses only under a neurologist.
    • A short course of corticosteroid bridges the weeks until verapamil works: for example, prednisolone 50 to 60 mg orally daily for 5 days, then tapered over about 2 weeks (per eTG), while verapamil is titrated.
    • Lithium, topiramate and greater occipital nerve block are further options through a neurologist (galcanezumab is used overseas but is not approved for cluster headache in Australia).
  • Lifestyle:
    • Stop smoking: give brief advice, refer to Quitline (13 7848) and offer pharmacotherapy.
    • Avoid alcohol during a bout, as it can trigger attacks.
    • Keep a headache diary.
  • Referral: neurology.
  • Mood: the attacks are so severe that they affect mental health. Ask about mood and thoughts of self-harm, and treat depression promptly if present.

Safety netting

  • Call 000 or go to ED: a sudden severe headache unlike his usual attacks; fever with a stiff neck or rash; new weakness, numbness, vision loss, trouble speaking or confusion; a headache that changes pattern or does not settle; chest pain after sumatriptan that persists.
  • If he feels hopeless or has thoughts of self-harm: see the GP promptly, call Lifeline (13 11 14), or call 000 in an emergency.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks with an ECG before each verapamil increase, the neurology appointment, the headache diary, and written information.
points: Strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, at the same time each day, with tearing, a red eye, a runny or blocked nose on the same side and restlessness, is cluster headache. Patients with migraine lie still, while patients with cluster headache pace.
Ask about the autonomic features directly, and inspect the eyes during an attack. A partial Horner's syndrome on the side of the pain is common during attacks.

Waking from sleep is a red flag to explore, not to dismiss. Clockwork attacks that resolve completely are typical of cluster headache. A progressive morning headache with vomiting or papilloedema suggests raised intracranial pressure.
Image a first presentation of cluster-like headache with MRI, because pituitary and cavernous sinus lesions can mimic it. Bloods do not help.

Treat attacks with 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather for 15 minutes, or sumatriptan 6 mg SC, not oral analgesics. Prevent attacks during a bout with verapamil, checking an ECG before each dose increase, and bridge with a short course of steroids.
Address smoking (especially near oxygen), alcohol during a bout and mood: cluster headache takes a heavy psychological toll.
